lesson.title: Headers: The Instructions That Travel Ahead of the Data
lesson.summary: A header is a block of control information placed at the front of a unit of data, telling network equipment and software how to handle whatever follows it.
lesson.body:
Imagine mailing a letter with no envelope, no address, and no stamp, just the pages themselves dropped into a mailbox. The postal system would have no way to know where it came from, where it should go, or even where one letter ends and another begins. A header solves exactly this problem for digital communication. It is a small, precisely structured block of bytes placed at the beginning of a unit of data that tells everything downstream how to treat the bytes that follow.

Headers are built from bytes arranged in fixed, agreed upon positions, which is why understanding the byte as a unit of measure matters so much here. A header is not free form text, it is a rigid layout where, for example, "the first 4 bits mean this" and "bytes 13 through 16 mean that." Both the sender and every piece of equipment that touches the data along the way must agree on this layout in advance, otherwise the bits are just noise. This rigid, byte level precision is what lets a router or a network card process millions of headers per second without ever having to guess.

A concrete example makes this tangible. Every IPv4 packet begins with a header that is, in the ordinary case, exactly 20 bytes long. Within those 20 bytes, specific byte positions are reserved for the source address, the destination address, a time to live value that prevents packets from circulating forever, and a field identifying which higher level protocol, such as TCP or UDP, produced the data inside. A router reading an IP header does not need to understand anything about the actual content being delivered. It only needs to read a handful of fixed byte positions to decide where to send the packet next.

Headers exist at nearly every layer of a network conversation, and each one typically adds its own header aimed at the concerns relevant to that layer. An Ethernet header carries physical network addresses relevant to the local network segment. A TCP header carries port numbers and sequence numbers relevant to reliable delivery between two programs. Each header is added by a different piece of software or hardware, and each one is read and then usually removed by its counterpart at the receiving end, a pairing of software components that never has to inspect any other layer's header to do its own job correctly.

It is worth being precise about what a header is not. It is not the actual content the sender cares about, that is the payload, covered next. The header is metadata about that content: instructions for handling it, not the thing itself. A mail carrier reads the envelope, not the letter inside, to decide where to deliver it, and network equipment behaves the same way, reading only headers whenever possible and leaving the enclosed content untouched. This distinction between the instructions and the cargo they describe becomes essential once you look at how headers and payloads are combined through encapsulation to build the packets that actually travel across real networks.
